fixes.explanation: That's right. David says, “I cry out by day, O my God, but You do not answer…” So in this moment, he isn't hearing an answer. He says it honestly, and he keeps talking to God anyway. And he says he has no rest by night, which I think is a hard combination.

Delivered. David says, “In You our fathers trusted; they trusted and You delivered them.” Then the next verse says they cried out and were set free. David is looking back at what God has done before. When you're stuck, a good memory can be the best thing in your pocket.

Right. David says, “From birth I was cast upon You; from my mother’s womb You have been my God.” That's from the very start of his life. A crown has nothing to do with it. God has been his God since his mother's womb.

That's the reason. David says, “Be not far from me, for trouble is near and there is no one to help.” He doesn't ask for anything fancy. He asks God not to be far, because there is no one to help. I think that's a prayer a lot of us have prayed.

Yes. Water poured out can't be gathered back up, and wax goes soft in the heat. David also says his strength is “…dried up like a potsherd…” (a piece of broken pottery). Put those pictures together and you see a man who is weak and worn out. I think he's saying he feels drained.

Not this time. David says his bones are disjointed and his strength is “…dried up like a potsherd…” Those pictures describe someone who is weak, not someone getting ready to fight. He also says his heart is like wax, melting away within him.

His clothing. David says, “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” They are dividing his garments among themselves. It's a cold moment, and I think it hurts. Casting lots was a way of choosing who got what, and here it's used on a man's clothing.

Not this one, baker. There's no crown in this verse at all. David says, “They divide my garments among them and cast lots for my clothing.” It's his clothing they cast lots for. I think that makes the moment feel even more stripped down.

Not this one, baker. David doesn't mention his name in this verse. He says, “Deliver my soul from the sword, my precious life from the power of wild dogs.” It's his life he asks God to save. That's the thing he calls precious.
The poor. David says, “The poor will eat and be satisfied; those who seek the LORD will praise Him.” They don't just eat, they eat and are satisfied. I think that's a lovely promise to hear.
Not quite, baker. David doesn't say kings in this verse. He says, “The poor will eat and be satisfied…” It's the poor he names as the ones who eat and are satisfied.
